challenges.name: metric-cardinality-quiz
challenges.title: How many series will this label create?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the metrics backend: the label counts of the request counter before a proposed change, and the /metrics output after a release that labelled requests with the raw path.

questions.question:
PromQL on the request counter today:

count(http_server_requests_total)                                   => 820
count(count by (route) (http_server_requests_total))                => 41
count(count by (method) (http_server_requests_total))               => 5
count(count by (status_class) (http_server_requests_total))         => 4

A pull request adds one label so marketing can see traffic per course:

requests.add(1, { route, method, status_class, course_slug });   // 300 published courses today

Statement: "In the worst case this counter goes from 820 series to about 246,000, because every existing combination can now be split by each of the 300 course slugs."
questions.explanation: True. A series is one unique combination of label values, so the series count of a metric is bounded by the product of the number of values of each label. Each of the 820 combinations that exist today can appear with each of the 300 slugs: 820 x 300 = 246,000 in the worst case. The real number is usually lower, because course_slug only shows up on course routes, but the bound grows with every published course and the backend pays for each combination that does occur. The misconception is that adding one label adds its number of values (+300); it multiplies.

questions.question:
/metrics on one API instance after a release that labels requests with the raw path:

http_server_requests_total{path="/courses/42/lessons/7",method="GET",status="200"} 1
http_server_requests_total{path="/courses/42/lessons/8",method="GET",status="200"} 2
http_server_requests_total{path="/reset/3f2b8c1e-9a4d-4e7b-8c21-0d5e6f7a8b9c",method="POST",status="204"} 1
http_server_requests_total{path="/courses/react-hooks?utm_source=newsletter",method="GET",status="200"} 1
... (38,000 more lines)

Prometheus: prometheus_tsdb_head_series 1.2M (140k before the release)
Requests per day: 2.1M before and after the release

Statement: "Traffic did not grow and most of these series have a count of 1 or 2, so they add almost nothing to the memory and the bill of the metrics backend."
questions.explanation: False. The cost of a metrics backend follows the number of active series, not the number of requests: each series has its own index entry, its own chunks in memory and its own samples on every scrape, whether its value is 1 or 1,000,000, and many hosted backends bill per active series. Head series went from 140k to 1.2M with the same traffic, which is exactly the problem. Queries also get slower, because sum by (route) now has to read hundreds of thousands of series. The misconception is to think a counter that rarely increments is cheap; a series costs about the same from the moment it exists.

challenges.name: metric-cardinality-guard
challenges.title: A cardinality guard for metric labels
challenges.description:
After a release labelled the request counter with raw paths, the CodeDev metrics backend went from 140k to 1.2M active series. Write the guard every metric point now goes through before it is exported: recordAll(points, maxValuesPerLabel) returns the output lines, with the helpers routeTemplate(path) and statusClass(status).

For each point, in input order:
1. Reject it (count it, record nothing) when metric is not a non-empty string or value is not a finite number >= 0.
2. Normalise its labels (a missing labels object means no labels): drop the forbidden labels user_id, email and session_id and every label whose value is ""; replace path with route = routeTemplate(path), except when the point already has a non-empty route label, which is kept (path is then dropped); status keeps its name and becomes statusClass(status); every other label is kept as is.
3. Cap: for each metric and each label name separately, the first maxValuesPerLabel distinct values (after step 2, in the order the points arrive) are kept. A value already kept stays; a new value when that many are already kept becomes "other", and that label name is reported as capped for that metric.
4. Add value to its series: the metric plus all its labels after steps 2 and 3.

routeTemplate(path): cut at the first ? or #, split on /, drop empty segments, replace a segment made only of digits with :id and a UUID (8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal digits, any case) with :uuid, keep other segments, join with a leading / ("/" when nothing is left). "/courses/42/lessons/7/?tab=hints" -> "/courses/:id/lessons/:id". statusClass(status): a three-digit code from 100 to 599 -> first digit + "xx" ("404" -> "4xx"), anything else -> "unknown".

Input (stdin, JSON): { "maxValuesPerLabel": 3, "points": [{ "metric": "http_server_requests_total", "value": 1, "labels": { "path": "/courses/42", "method": "GET", "status": "200", "user_id": "u_17" } }] }. Output lines: one per series in Prometheus text format, metric{name="value",...} total, label names sorted (just "metric total" without labels), lines sorted by the text before the total in plain string order; then per metric in sorted order "# <metric>: <n> series, capped: <capped label names sorted, joined with ", ">" (or "capped: none"); last "# total: <n> series, <r> rejected".
hints: Which of these labels can take a new value every time a new learner, a new course or a new link shows up, and which can only take a handful of values whatever happens? The guard has to turn the first kind into the second, and the cap is the safety net for what the rules did not foresee.

Keep three things apart: normalising a point's labels (forbidden labels, empty values, path to route, status to class), the cap (it works on normalised values and needs its own memory per metric and per label name, filled in arrival order) and the output (series text with sorted label names, then the sorted lines and the summary). Check whether your cap runs before or after the route template: the order changes which values are kept.

A worked example with other data, maxValuesPerLabel 2 and a label region: the points arrive with region eu, us, eu, ap, sa, us. eu and us are kept, so they stay eu and us every time; ap and sa arrive when two values are already kept and both become other. The metric then has three series for region (eu, us, other) and reports region as capped. A second metric with its own region label starts with an empty list.
